title: What fetch and push actually do: refspecs
summary: Every fetch and push is a refspec — a source, a destination and a plus sign. Read the one in your config, then write your own to fetch a single branch or push to a differently-named one.
mental_model: A refspec is `<src>:<dst>`, optionally prefixed with `+` meaning 'allow non-fast-forward'. `git fetch origin` is shorthand for the refspec sitting in your config; everything else in remotes is that one pattern applied differently.

steps.title: Read the refspec you already have
steps.why: Cloning wrote this line into `.git/config`. It says: fetch every ref under refs/heads on the remote, and store each under refs/remotes/origin. That is why `origin/main` exists and where it comes from.

steps.title: Take it apart
steps.why: `+` allow non-fast-forward updates. `refs/heads/*` the source pattern on the remote. `refs/remotes/origin/*` where to put each match locally. Three parts, and every remote operation uses them.
steps.expect: ls-remote shows the server's raw refs; branch -r shows where the refspec filed them.

steps.title: Fetch one branch into a name of your choosing
steps.why: A refspec on the command line overrides the configured one. Here the server's feature/alpha lands in a ref called `review/alpha` — useful when reviewing someone's branch without cluttering your remote-tracking namespace.

verify.label: the branch was fetched under a different name

steps.title: Push to a differently-named remote branch
steps.why: `src:dst` on push works the same way. Your local `main` can be published as `staging` on the server without renaming anything locally — this is how deploy-by-push setups work.
steps.expect: A new staging branch on the server pointing at your main.

verify.label: main was published under a different name

steps.title: Delete by pushing nothing
steps.why: An empty source means 'make the destination not exist'. `git push origin --delete x` is a friendlier spelling of `git push origin :x`, and now you can see why the colon form works.

verify.label: an empty source deleted the remote ref

steps.title: Narrow the configured refspec
steps.why: Replacing the wildcard with a single branch makes every future `git fetch` cheap and quiet — the basis of a single-branch clone. Set it back afterwards, or you will wonder why new branches never appear.
steps.expect: Only main is fetched from now on.

steps.title: Add a second refspec instead of replacing
steps.why: A remote can have several fetch refspecs. `--add` appends one, which is how you fetch pull-request refs from GitHub (`+refs/pull/*/head:refs/remotes/origin/pr/*`) alongside the usual branches.

verify.label: the remote has two fetch refspecs configured
the wildcard refspec is restored and fetching every branch again
you fetched a remote branch into a local name of your choosing
the branch you published under another name was deleted with an empty-source refspec
the wildcard refspec fetches every branch again

pitfalls: Narrowing `remote.origin.fetch` is what `--single-branch` does. If new branches stop appearing after a clone, this config line is why.
Without a `+`, a fetch that would move a ref backwards is refused. The plus is what lets remote-tracking refs follow a force-push.
`git push origin main` uses `push.default` to decide the destination. Writing `main:refs/heads/main` explicitly removes all ambiguity.
Fetching GitHub pull requests needs `+refs/pull/*/head:refs/remotes/origin/pr/*` — a refspec, not a special feature.
cheatsheet: the refspec you already use every day
fetch one ref into a name you choose
empty source deletes the remote ref
the server's raw refs, no cache involved
fetch more, such as PR refs
